chunks.text: One bright morning, King Janaka rose to greet the sage Vishwamitra and the two sons of Dasaratha, Rama and Lakshmana, after he had performed his daily devotions. He bowed to the sage with all reverence and asked what he might do for him, saying he was ready to be commanded.

Vishwamitra answered that these famed Kshatriyas, sons of Dasaratha, longed to see the great bow that lay in Janaka's keeping, and asked that it be shown to them, so that their desire might be satisfied and they could return content.

Janaka told the sage the story of the bow. A king named Devarata, elder brother of Nimi, had once held it in trust. Long before, when the mighty Shiva meant to destroy the sacrifice of Daksha, he had drawn this very bow and declared to the gods in anger that since they denied him his share of the offering, he would sever their heads with it.
The frightened gods hastened to appease him, and Shiva, pleased with them, gave the bow into their keeping; it passed at last, as a trust, to Janaka's ancestor.

Janaka then told of his daughter. As he was ploughing the sacrificial ground, a maiden had risen from the earth; he found her while hallowing the field, and she became known as Sita, growing up as his own daughter though she had not come to him by the usual course of birth. Her hand, Janaka had determined, could only be won by whoever could bend the great bow.

Many kings had come to Mithila to seek her, but because her dower was to be proven strength alone, Janaka would not give her to any who asked. All the assembled kings tried their strength upon the bow, but not one of them could so much as hold or wield it, and Janaka turned them all away as too weak.

Enraged at their failure, the kings besieged Mithila and harried the city for a year, until Janaka's defenses were exhausted and he was sorely troubled. He prayed to the gods, who granted him a fourfold army, and with it the wicked kings were routed, broken and scattered in every direction, their strength and confidence gone.
Now, Janaka said, he would show this same bow to Rama and Lakshmana, and if Rama could fix the string to it, he would give his daughter Sita to Dasaratha's son.

Hearing this, Vishwamitra asked Janaka to show the bow to Rama, and the king commanded his ministers to bring it forth, adorned with garlands and unguents. The ministers entered the city and returned bearing the bow in an iron case set upon an eight-wheeled cart, a weight so great that five thousand powerful men could only draw it along with difficulty.
The royal counsellors declared it the best of bows, worshipped by every sovereign, and asked Janaka whether he wished it shown.

With his palms joined, Janaka told Vishwamitra, Rama, and Lakshmana that this bow had always been worshipped by his line, and that not gods, Asuras, Rakshasas, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Kinnaras, nor the mighty serpent-lords had ever managed to string it, stretch it, fix an arrow to it, pull its string, or wield it at all — how then should mortal men?

Vishwamitra bade Rama look upon the bow. Rama opened the case, gazed at it, and asked whether he should touch this divine bow with his hand and attempt to wield and draw it; both the king and the sage told him to go ahead. Before countless thousands of onlookers, Rama took hold of the bow at its middle with such ease that he seemed unburdened by it, fixed the string, drew it back, and snapped the great bow in two.

The sound of its breaking was as mighty as a thunderclap; the earth shook as though a mountain were splitting apart, and the noise overwhelmed the crowd so that everyone but the sage, the king, and the two sons of Raghu fell to the ground.

When the people had recovered themselves, Janaka, his fears gone, folded his hands and told Vishwamitra that he had witnessed Rama's prowess, a thing so wonderful he had not believed it possible. His daughter Sita, he said, joined to Dasaratha's son, would bring glory to Janaka's line, and his promise to give her to whoever bent the bow was now fulfilled; he would give Sita, dearer to him than life itself, to Rama.

With Vishwamitra's leave, he asked that his counsellors be sent at once by chariot to Ayodhya, to tell King Dasaratha of the bestowal of Sita upon Rama and of the welfare of the two princes under the sage's protection, and to bring the king back with them. Vishwamitra agreed, and Janaka summoned his counsellors and sent them to Ayodhya with his letter, to tell the king everything and bring him to Mithila.
